title: Asking with onko
summary: Add the yes/no question ending -ko to on: on + -ko = onko. Use onko with every owner, including meillä, teillä, and heillä.
objectives: Form a possession question with onko for any owner.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Add the yes/no question ending -ko to on: on + -ko = onko. Use onko with every owner, including meillä, teillä, and heillä.

This pack models questions about one thing with its basic noun form, such as Onko sinulla pallo? A partitive question such as Onko sinulla palloa? is also natural when asking whether a ball is available. Tasks show the intended noun form.
Hänellä can refer to a man or a woman. Sinulla addresses one person; teillä addresses a group in these tasks. Teillä can also address one person politely when that context is stated.
A statement becomes a question by changing fixed on to onko and putting it first; retain the possessor and basic noun.
keyPoints: Use one singular thing and the owner form shown by the prompt.

steps: Start with on (“have” here) and add the yes/no question ending -ko: on + -ko = onko.
minulla means “I as the owner”. Put the owner after onko.
kirja (“book”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
The question word remains onko with sinulla; do not use oletko from an “Are you …?” sentence.
sinulla means “you as the owner” for one person. Put the owner after onko.
koira (“dog”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
Onko stays the same whether hänellä is translated with “he” or “she”.
hänellä means “he as the owner” or “she as the owner”; this example uses “she”. Put the owner after onko.
auto (“car”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
Several owners do not require olemmeko. Possession still begins with onko.
meillä means “we as the owner”. Put the owner after onko.
pallo (“ball”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
The group owner teillä does not require oletteko; keep onko.
teillä means “you as the owner” for a group. Put the owner after onko.
kynä (“pen”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
Heillä does not require ovatko. The possession question still uses onko.
heillä means “they as the owner”. Put the owner after onko.
peli (“game”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
Changing the noun changes what is asked about, not onko.
sinulla means “you as the owner” for one person. Put the owner after onko.
kissa (“cat”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
The noun’s front vowels do not change onko to onkö; the question ending attaches to on.
heillä means “they as the owner”. Put the owner after onko.
tyyny (“pillow”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.

commonMistakes: Add -ko to fixed on to form onko; plural owners do not require olemmeko or ovatko.
Put Onko before the owner: Onko sinulla pallo? The statement Sinulla on pallo is not the requested question.
Keep the noun form shown in the task. This pack models basic singular nouns; partitive questions are also natural in other contexts.
